versionNotes: 2026-07-31 — first functional-language seed file (fixed/social-purpose phrases, e.g. introductions, spelling requests, service transactions). Classified under Speaking (speaking.functional_phrases subskill), not Vocabulary, per the container/leaf redesign decision.
Every leaf's lessonBody/examples/exercises/questions are newly authored.

leaves.title: Understanding and practicing short social exchanges
leaves.lessonBody: Short, everyday spoken exchanges combine several functions at once — ordering something, introducing yourself, and clarifying a name that wasn't heard clearly. Listen for the key words (the item ordered, the name given) even when the exchange has several speakers. Common clarification phrases: 'Sorry, what was that?', 'Did you say...?', 'No, it's [name], not [name].'
examples: A: A coffee, please. B: What's your name? A: Marco. B: Marco, coffee's ready!
A: Are you Elena? B: No, I'm not. I'm Farah. A: Oh sorry! B: No problem.
A: Hello! Are you Mr. Diallo? B: Yes, I am. Nice to meet you.
commonMistakes: Don't assume you heard a name correctly the first time — asking for clarification is normal and polite.
'Sorry, what was that?' is more natural than 'Repeat, please' in casual conversation.

exercises.title: Complete the exchange
exercises.instructions: Read each short exchange and complete the missing line.

questions.prompt: A: Are you Sofia? B: No, I'm ___. I'm Farah.
A: A tea, please. B: What's your ___? A: Leo.
A: Sorry, what was ___? B: I said Diallo.

exercises.instructions: Choose the most natural next line in each exchange.

A: Hello, is your name Chen? B: ___

leaves.title: Understanding classroom instructions
leaves.lessonBody: Common instructions a teacher gives in class: 'Open your books.', 'Close your books.', 'Stand up, please.', 'Sit down, please.', 'Look at the board, please.', 'Go to page...' Common phrases a student uses: 'How do you spell it?', 'Sorry, can you repeat that, please?', 'I don't understand.', 'I don't know.'
examples: Teacher: Open your books to page five, please.
Student: Sorry, can you repeat that, please?
commonMistakes: 'Sorry?' alone is a polite, common way to ask someone to repeat something — you don't always need a full sentence.
'I don't know' answers a question you can't answer; 'I don't understand' means the instruction itself was unclear — they aren't interchangeable.

exercises.title: Match the instruction to its purpose
exercises.instructions: Choose what the teacher wants the student to do.

leaves.title: Introducing yourself
leaves.lessonBody: Fixed phrases for introducing yourself and meeting someone new: 'Hi, I'm...', 'What's your name?', 'Nice to meet you.'
examples: A: Hi, I'm Priya. B: Hi, I'm Marco. Nice to meet you.
A: What's your name? B: I'm Felix.
commonMistakes: Don't answer 'What's your name?' with just a name — a full response like 'I'm Felix' is more natural in this context.

exercises.title: Choose the best response
exercises.instructions: Choose the most natural response to complete each exchange.

questions.prompt: A: Hi, I'm Sara. What's your name? B: ___
A: Nice to meet you. B: ___
A: Hello, I'm Mr. Cho. B: ___
A: What's your name? B: ___

leaves.title: Saying goodbye
leaves.lessonBody: Fixed phrases for ending a conversation: 'Goodbye' / 'Bye', 'See you tomorrow.', 'See you on Monday.'
examples: A: Bye! See you tomorrow. B: Bye!
A: See you on Friday. B: OK, see you then.
commonMistakes: 'Goodbye' and 'Bye' both work, but don't mix them with 'Hello' at the end of a conversation.

exercises.title: Complete the goodbye
exercises.instructions: Complete each goodbye exchange with the correct phrase.

questions.prompt: A: Bye! ___ tomorrow. B: Bye!
A: See you on ___. (the day after Sunday)
A: ___! B: Goodbye, have a nice day.

leaves.title: Spelling and the alphabet
leaves.lessonBody: Fixed phrases for asking about spelling: 'How do you spell that?', 'Can you spell your last name, please?' Answers are given letter by letter, e.g. 'W-A-L-K-E-R.'
examples: A: How do you spell your last name? B: It's W-A-L-K-E-R.
A: Sorry, can you spell that, please? B: Sure, it's M-A-R-C-O.
commonMistakes: Say letters one at a time when spelling, not as a whole word.
'How do you spell it?' is more natural than 'What is the spelling?' in everyday speech.

exercises.title: Choose the best response
exercises.instructions: Choose the most natural response to complete each exchange.

questions.prompt: A: How do you spell your last name? B: ___
A: Sorry, can you spell that, please? B: ___
A: ___? B: It's spelled S-M-I-T-H.

leaves.title: Service requests (hotels and restaurants)
leaves.lessonBody: Fixed phrases for common service situations: 'I have a reservation.', 'A table for two, please.', 'Can I have the check, please?' Staff often reply with 'Sure,' 'Right this way,' or 'Just a moment.'
examples: A: I have a reservation. My name's Aliyah Reed. B: Let me check... Yes, you're in room 214.
A: A table for two, please. B: Right this way.
commonMistakes: 'I have a reservation' is more natural than 'I reserved' when checking in.
'A table for two, please' doesn't need a full sentence like 'I want a table for two.'

exercises.title: Complete the exchange
exercises.instructions: Complete each short exchange with the correct phrase.

questions.prompt: A: Hello, how can I help you? B: Hi, I ___ a reservation. My name's Noah Kim.
A: A table for ___, please. B: Right this way.
A: Can I ___ the check, please? B: Of course.
